title: Judges 2:1–5
context: The LORD’s angel comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and speaks in the first person. He has brought Israel out of Egypt and into the land sworn to the fathers, and he has said that he will never break his covenant with them. They were to make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land and to break down their altars, but they have not listened to his voice. Therefore he also said that he will not drive those nations out from before them; they shall be in Israel’s sides, and their gods will be a snare. When the angel has spoken these words to all the children of Israel, the people lift up their voice and weep. They call the place Bochim and sacrifice there to the LORD. Both traditions take the speech as the LORD’s own indictment of the incomplete obedience just narrated. The identity of the LORD’s angel is debated: some read a theophany, the LORD himself appearing as the angel; some read a heavenly messenger who speaks God’s words in the first person; some Christian readers have also heard a Christophany. Those are interpretive options, not a consensus and not an Arminian–Reformed contrast. Gilgal recalls the entry into the land; the movement from there to a place of weeping is a literary fact of the scene, not a secret code that must be forced.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel came up from Gilgal to Bochim. He said, “I brought you out of Egypt, and have brought you to the land which I swore to give your fathers. I said, ‘I will never break my covenant with you.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD’s angel” came up from Gilgal to Bochim. He said that he brought them out of Egypt and to the land he swore to give their fathers, and, “I will never break my covenant with you.” The speech begins with redemption, gift, and an unbreakable covenant.

Arminian readers hear God binding himself and then addressing this people in their actual hearing. Who the angel is remains an open interpretive question; the words are to be received as the LORD’s, and Israel is truly called to remember what he has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the first-person speech as the LORD’s own claim: he brought them out, he brought them in, and he will never break his covenant. Whether one reads the LORD’s angel as a theophany, as a messenger who speaks for God, or, as some Christians have, as a Christophany, the identity should be held as an option, not as a settled consensus, and not as a fork between the two traditions.

Both receive the verse as God’s faithful recitation of his saving work and his covenant, shared ground for the charge that follows.

verses.text: You shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land. You shall break down their altars.’ But you have not listened to my voice. Why have you done this?
verses.arminianNotes:
The quoted charge continues: “You shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land. You shall break down their altars.” Then the accusation: “But you have not listened to my voice. Why have you done this?” Chapter 1’s compromises are now named as covenant-making and as a refusal to listen.

Arminian readers hear a real why. God is not asking because he lacks knowledge; classical Arminianism affirms his exhaustive foreknowledge. The question is a judicial and moral appeal to a people who have actually refused his voice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same unkept commands and the same “Why have you done this?” The inquiry is not a gap in God’s knowledge; it is the form of an indictment. What chapter 1 showed in lists is here called not listening to his voice.

Both traditions take the verse as a true charge against partial obedience, shared ground, without reading the question as if the future or the past were unknown to God.

verses.text: Therefore I also said, ‘I will not drive them out from before you; but they shall be in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore he also said, “I will not drive them out from before you; but they shall be in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you.” The leftover nations are now announced as God’s own settled response, and as a spiritual danger.

Arminian readers hear a real consequence of not listening. God will not drive the nations out; they will press Israel, and their gods will snare a people who would not break the altars down. The outcome matches the choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that this withholding is something God also said. Israel’s failure in chapter 1 and the LORD’s decision not to drive the nations out belong together: the nations left in their sides are both a judgment and a snare.

Both traditions read the verse as the theological key to the unfinished map, not as a contrast that sets human failure against divine purpose as if only one were true.

verses.text: When the LORD’s angel spoke these words to all the children of Israel, the people lifted up their voice and wept.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the LORD’s angel spoke these words to all the children of Israel, the people lifted up their voice and wept. The indictment is public, and the first response is tears.

Arminian readers hear a right grief in the moment. The whole people is addressed, and they actually weep; whether that weeping becomes lasting obedience is a question the rest of the chapter will press, not a verdict this verse itself pronounces.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the lifted voice and the weeping as the immediate fruit of the word. All Israel hears, and all Israel weeps. The next verses will show a sacrifice at this place; later verses will show how quickly another generation departs.

Both traditions receive the tears as a real response to God’s charge, without declaring in advance that they are either shallow or complete repentance, and without a contrast between the two readings.

verses.text: They called the name of that place Bochim, and they sacrificed there to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
They called the name of that place Bochim, and they sacrificed there to the LORD. The site is named after the weeping just described, and worship is offered to the LORD, not to the Baals.

Arminian readers hear a memorial and a sacrifice that match the tears of verse 4. They name the place and they turn, in this scene, to the LORD; the book will still have to ask what comes of this grief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same two acts: a name that remembers the weeping, and a sacrifice to the LORD at that place. The narrator does not locate Bochim on the map, and the site should not be fixed as if a consensus had settled it.

Both traditions take the naming and the sacrifice as a true response in the scene, shared ground at the close of the indictment.
